topic.resolution: Apart from minor variants that change no teaching or story, the text in modern critical Bibles accurately reproduces the earliest recoverable form of each book.
topic.question: How accurately has the text of the Bible been transmitted from its earliest recoverable form to today?
topic.claim: Apart from minor variants that change no teaching or story, the text in modern critical Bibles accurately reproduces the earliest recoverable form of each book.

analyses.verdict: Mostly well preserved, but the claim is too strong
analyses.bottom_line: Much of the Bible can be reconstructed with considerable confidence, and most variants are small. But some ancient variants change narrative details or the wording of passages with theological significance. I score the claim as referring to the main text printed in modern critical editions or translations, compared with the best-supported recoverable earlier text—not necessarily the lost original manuscript. On that reading, its assertion that remaining differences are only minor is unlikely: some critical editions deliberately print a particular manuscript tradition even where substantial earlier alternatives survive. Editions and translations often identify such issues in brackets or notes, so this is not a claim that they conceal them.

sub_claims.claim: Much biblical wording has been transmitted with substantial fidelity.
sub_claims.case_for: Numerous manuscripts and ancient translations allow comparison across places and centuries; most identifiable differences are spelling, word order, or other relatively small changes.
sub_claims.case_against: Witnesses are unevenly distributed across books and periods, and agreement among later manuscripts cannot guarantee that an earlier shared reading was correct.
sub_claims.consensus: Broadly accepted by textual critics, including confessional scholars, though estimates of certainty vary by passage and book.
evidence: Dead Sea Scroll biblical manuscripts provide Hebrew witnesses many centuries older than the medieval manuscripts underlying standard printed Hebrew texts.
The New Testament survives in thousands of Greek manuscripts, alongside early translations and quotations.
Manuscript numbers alone do not measure independence or establish the earliest reading.
sub_claims.verdict: Very likely true as a generalization, not a guarantee for every passage.

sub_claims.claim: All significant ancient variants are minor and change no story or teaching.
sub_claims.case_for: Most variants are minor, and many substantial additions or omissions are recognizable and marked in modern editions. No major Christian doctrine necessarily stands or falls on a single disputed passage.
sub_claims.case_against: Some variants add or remove whole episodes or alter the depiction of divine beings or Jesus. Whether an established doctrine ultimately changes is a different question from whether a passage's story or teaching changes.
sub_claims.consensus: Scholars across confessional and nonconfessional traditions generally acknowledge consequential variants, while disagreeing about individual readings and their theological importance.
evidence: Mark 16:9–20 contains resurrection appearances absent from some early witnesses and is bracketed in the standard Nestle-Aland critical Greek text.
John 7:53–8:11, the woman accused of adultery, is absent from some early witnesses and bracketed in that edition.
Deuteronomy 32:8 has 'sons of Israel' in the Masoretic Hebrew tradition, while a Dead Sea Scroll witness supports 'sons of God'; the Greek tradition reads 'angels of God.'
sub_claims.verdict: Almost certainly false.

sub_claims.claim: The main text of every modern critical Bible reproduces the best-supported earlier form apart from minor differences.
sub_claims.case_for: Critical editions use manuscript evidence systematically, and translations frequently adopt earlier readings over later traditional ones. Brackets and apparatuses alert readers to important uncertainties.
sub_claims.case_against: Some critical editions intentionally print a particular manuscript rather than an eclectic reconstruction, and major disputed passages can remain in the main text with qualification. A textual decision in one passage may also remain genuinely debatable.
sub_claims.consensus: There is no consensus that every printed reading is the best reconstruction. Scholars generally recognize the different aims of diplomatic editions, eclectic editions, and translations.
evidence: Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia principally prints the medieval Leningrad Codex rather than replacing its text wherever another witness may preserve an earlier reading.
Before 1 Samuel 11:1, a Dead Sea Scroll manuscript preserves a substantial account of Nahash's oppression that is missing from the Masoretic text; Josephus also knows a related account.
Nestle-Aland prints the longer ending of Mark and the adultery episode in double brackets, signaling their disputed status rather than presenting them as secure.
sub_claims.verdict: Unlikely under the stated main-text reading; notes and editorial brackets materially qualify the examples.

sub_claims.claim: Every biblical book has one recoverable earliest form that scholars can confidently identify.
sub_claims.case_for: Comparing independent witnesses can often identify likely earlier readings and reconstruct much of an early text.
sub_claims.case_against: Evidence may run out before the earliest stages, and some books circulated in more than one ancient literary edition. The earliest surviving or reconstructible form need not be the author's final wording.
sub_claims.consensus: Scholars broadly recognize substantial uncertainty and ancient textual plurality; they differ about how confidently particular early forms can be reconstructed and what counts as the target text.
evidence: The Greek Jeremiah is substantially shorter and arranged differently from the Masoretic Hebrew version.
Some Dead Sea Scroll Jeremiah manuscripts support a Hebrew textual form related to the shorter Greek edition.
No original biblical manuscripts are known to survive.
sub_claims.verdict: Unlikely as a universal claim.

cruxes.crux: Does the claim concern printed main text, or the edition together with its brackets and notes?
cruxes.if_yes: If main text alone is meant, substantial disputed or omitted material counts against the claim.
cruxes.if_no: If the complete annotated edition is meant, its presentation of uncertainty is much stronger, though it still does not make all variants minor.
cruxes.your_view: I score the main-text reading and distinguish an editor's deliberate reproduction of a manuscript from an editorial mistake.

cruxes.crux: Does any substantial narrative or theological difference count as changing a story or teaching?
cruxes.if_yes: The added or omitted episodes and the Nahash passage make the claim very unlikely.
cruxes.if_no: If only changes to an entire overarching narrative or an established doctrine count, the claim becomes more defensible but much less precise.
cruxes.your_view: An added episode or materially different narrative background is more than a minor variant, even if the broader religion is unchanged.

cruxes.crux: Can the earlier form of a disputed passage be established from the available witnesses?
cruxes.if_yes: A modern main text that prints a substantially different reading is a counterexample.
cruxes.if_no: The existence of a substantive variant alone does not prove which printed reading departs from the earliest recoverable form.
cruxes.your_view: Some cases have strong evidence for an earlier reading, but others remain genuinely contested.

cruxes.crux: Is the target the earliest recoverable text or the lost authorial original?
cruxes.if_yes: For the recoverable text, surviving witnesses constrain the comparison, although editorial choices still matter.
cruxes.if_no: For the original wording, uncertainty is greater because the evidence may not reach back far enough and some books had complex histories.
cruxes.your_view: I use the recoverable-text target specified in the question, not an assumed perfect recovery of autographs.

strongest_for: Most identifiable variants are small, and comparison of many witnesses often yields a well-supported text.
Modern critical editions expose major uncertainty through apparatuses and brackets instead of simply perpetuating later additions.
Ancient witnesses sometimes confirm that long stretches of text were transmitted with substantial stability.
A meaningful textual difference does not automatically overturn a doctrine or the Bible's overall narrative.
strongest_against: Some variants involve whole episodes, not just spelling or insignificant wording.
The Masoretic text of Samuel omits substantial narrative background preserved in an ancient Hebrew witness.
Critical editions may intentionally print one textual tradition rather than silently reconstruct the earliest attainable text.
For some books, multiple ancient editions and limited evidence make a single confidently recoverable earliest form problematic.

for: Counting manuscripts alone proves the original text: witnesses may be late or related.
No doctrine depends on a variant, therefore no variant changes a teaching: those are different claims.
Divine preservation guarantees a particular printed wording: that is a theological premise, not independent manuscript evidence.
against: There are many variants, therefore the text is hopelessly corrupted: most are small and many are readily assessed.
A disputed reading proves the entire Bible is unreliable: uncertainty is passage-specific.
A modern edition prints a disputed passage, therefore its editors regard it as unquestionably original: brackets and notes can explicitly say otherwise.

would_change: Early, independent continuous manuscripts resolving major disputed passages and substantially changing the preferred reconstructions.
A persuasive demonstration that the longer Nahash account is an early expansion rather than material lost from the Masoretic tradition.
A clearly specified definition of 'critical Bibles' that treats annotated alternative readings, rather than the printed main text, as the text being assessed.

sources.citation: Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd edition, 2012
Eugene Ulrich, The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Origins of the Bible, 1999
Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd edition, 1994
Peter J. Gurry and Elijah Hixson, eds., Myths and Mistakes in New Testament Textual Criticism, 2019
Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia, 5th edition, 1997
Novum Testamentum Graece, 28th edition, 2012

analyses.label: GPT-6.1

analyses.verdict: False as stated: variants alter prominent stories and theological prooftexts, and modern Old Testaments translate medieval manuscripts rather than the earliest recoverable texts.
analyses.bottom_line: While modern textual criticism demonstrates that the broad historical substance and literary framework of the Bible have been transmitted with remarkable fidelity—with over 90% of the New Testament text firmly established—the claim fails on its specific assertions. Several famous and influential stories, including the Woman Caught in Adultery (John 7:53-8:11) and the Longer Ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20), are demonstrably secondary additions absent from the earliest recoverable text. Furthermore, while systematic Christian dogmas rarely depend on a single verse, individual variants directly alter significant theological statements regarding the Trinity, Christology, and atonement. Finally, modern Bibles do not actually reconstruct the 'earliest recoverable form' of the Old Testament; instead, they translate the medieval Masoretic Text (c. 1008 CE) with occasional footnotes, despite Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint evidence showing earlier, distinct literary editions for books like Jeremiah and Samuel.

sub_claims.claim: Modern critical editions of the New Testament (NA28/UBS5) accurately reconstruct the 2nd/3rd-century initial text for the overwhelming majority of the text.
sub_claims.case_for: Thousands of Greek manuscripts, early papyri (P45, P46, P66, P75), ancient versions, and patristic citations allow scholars using rigorous genealogical and eclectic methods (like the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method) to establish approximately 90-95% of the New Testament text beyond reasonable doubt.
sub_claims.case_against: Extant papyri only date to the late 2nd century at the earliest, leaving an undocumented period of decades where early scribes copied texts with considerable freedom; the 'initial text' (Ausgangstext) reconstructed by critics may represent a 2nd-century archetype rather than the original authorial autographs.
sub_claims.consensus: Broad consensus across both secular and confessional scholars that critical editions accurately reconstruct the earliest recoverable text to a very high degree of precision.
evidence: P52, P46, P66, and P75 dating from c. 175-250 CE
Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus from the 4th century CE
Over 5,800 cataloged Greek New Testament manuscripts showing broad genealogical convergence
sub_claims.verdict: Well-established textual consensus.

sub_claims.claim: Textual variants in biblical manuscripts change no major stories or narrative episodes.
sub_claims.case_for: The vast majority of textual variants (>95%) consist of spelling errors, accidental omissions, word-order variations, and synonyms that leave narrative storylines completely intact.
sub_claims.case_against: Major narrative episodes are incontrovertibly affected: the Pericope Adulterae (John 7:53-8:11) is absent from all early manuscripts; the Longer Ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) contains resurrection appearances, snake handling, and poison drinking not found in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus; the angel troubling the water (John 5:3b-4) is an interpolation; and the David and Goliath narrative in 1 Samuel 17 is nearly 45% longer in the Masoretic Text than in the early Septuagint.
sub_claims.consensus: Unanimous consensus among textual scholars that major narrative pericopes are textual additions or alterations.
evidence: Omission of John 7:53-8:11 in P66, P75, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus
Abrupt conclusion of Mark at 16:8 in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus
Omission of John 5:3b-4 in early Alexandrian witnesses
4QSam^a preserving an entire introductory narrative paragraph about Nahash the Ammonite gouging out eyes missing in the Masoretic Text of 1 Samuel 11
sub_claims.verdict: Definitively false.

sub_claims.claim: Textual variants do not alter any theological teachings or doctrinal propositions.
sub_claims.case_for: No cardinal dogma of Christianity or Judaism (e.g., the creation, the Exodus, monotheism, the crucifixion, or the resurrection) stands or falls on a single disputed variant; core theological doctrines are repeatedly affirmed across multiple undisputed passages.
sub_claims.case_against: While global systematic theology survives, localized teachings and key prooftexts are directly affected: the explicit Trinitarian formula in 1 John 5:7-8 (Comma Johanneum) is a late Latin insertion; Christological statements vary significantly between 'unique God' and 'only begotten Son' in John 1:18, and 'God' vs 'He who was revealed' in 1 Tim 3:16; Jesus' agony and bloody sweat (Luke 22:43-44) is textually disputed; and Mark 1:41 alternates between Jesus feeling 'compassion' or 'anger'.
sub_claims.consensus: Scholars agree that while sweeping systematic dogmas are preserved across the broader canon, specific theological assertions within individual books are substantially altered by variants.
evidence: Absence of the Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7-8) from all Greek manuscripts prior to the 10th century CE
Textual variation between 'monogenes theos' and 'monogenes huios' in John 1:18
Textual instability of Luke 22:43-44 and Luke 23:34a ('Father, forgive them')
Bart Ehrman's documentation of anti-adoptionist and anti-docetic scribal alterations in early manuscripts
sub_claims.verdict: False for localized teachings, though largely true for overarching canonical dogmas.

sub_claims.claim: Modern critical Bibles accurately reproduce the earliest recoverable form of each Old Testament book.
sub_claims.case_for: The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls demonstrated that the proto-Masoretic textual tradition was preserved with extraordinary precision for over a millennium, showing that the medieval Leningrad Codex is an exceptionally reliable witness to an ancient text-type.
sub_claims.case_against: Modern Bibles are diplomatic translations of the medieval Masoretic Text (specifically Codex Leningradensis, 1008 CE), not eclectic reconstructions of the earliest recoverable texts. The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint prove that several Old Testament books existed in distinct, earlier literary editions: the Septuagint and 4QJer^b preserve an edition of Jeremiah that is ~13% shorter and arranged differently than the Masoretic Text, yet modern Bibles print the longer, secondary Masoretic edition.
sub_claims.consensus: Strong consensus among Hebrew Bible scholars (e.g., Tov, Ulrich) that the Old Testament was textually pluriform and that modern Bibles print a single medieval Jewish standardization rather than an eclectic reconstruction of the earliest recoverable stage.
evidence: 4QJer^b and 4QJer^d aligning with the shorter, earlier Septuagint text of Jeremiah against the Masoretic Text
Divergent literary editions of Samuel, Kings, Exodus, and Proverbs attested at Qumran and in the Old Greek
Standard modern translations (NRSV, ESV, NIV) translating the Leningrad Codex as their base text rather than an eclectic critical reconstruction
sub_claims.verdict: Largely false due to modern reliance on the diplomatic Masoretic Text over earlier pluriform witnesses.

sub_claims.claim: The earliest recoverable textual form of each book is practically identical to the original authorial composition.
sub_claims.case_for: For New Testament epistles and Gospels, the chronological gap between composition (c. 50-95 CE) and our earliest substantial manuscript witnesses (c. 175-225 CE) is relatively narrow compared to other Greco-Roman historical literature, minimizing room for wholesale corruption.
sub_claims.case_against: For the Hebrew Bible, centuries of oral transmission, scribal redaction, linguistic updating, and composite literary development separate the historical events/authors from the earliest surviving manuscripts at Qumran (3rd century BCE). Even in the New Testament, early scribes copied texts before canonization when manuscripts were treated with less rigid word-for-word veneration.
sub_claims.consensus: Broad consensus that 'earliest recoverable text' is an archetype that often postdates authorial composition, especially for Old Testament composite books.
evidence: A multi-century gap between Old Testament compositional periods (Iron Age / Persian Period) and Qumran manuscripts (Hellenistic/Roman)
Documented editorial expansions across biblical books (e.g., post-Mosaic additions in Deuteronomy 34, multiple redactions in Isaiah)
Absence of 1st-century New Testament manuscript witnesses
sub_claims.verdict: Plausible for some New Testament epistles, but false for most of the Old Testament.

cruxes.crux: Does 'changing no teaching' refer to high-level systematic Christian/Jewish dogmas or to the specific theological claims of individual passages?
cruxes.if_yes: If it refers only to overarching dogmas (e.g., monotheism, the resurrection), the claim is mostly true because canonical redundancy protects general doctrines from single textual variants.
cruxes.if_no: If it refers to specific teachings, prooftexts, or ethics in individual passages (e.g., explicit Trinity proof, fasting, Christ's emotional state, submission), the claim is unequivocally false.
cruxes.your_view: Evaluating textual accuracy requires examining the specific claims of individual texts; retreating to canon-wide systematic dogmas moves the goalposts away from textual fidelity to doctrinal redundancy.

cruxes.crux: Do major narrative interpolations like John 7:53-8:11 and Mark 16:9-20 count as 'stories' that are changed by transmission?
cruxes.if_yes: The claim is flatly disproven, as two of the most widely recognized stories in the Gospels are textual additions not found in the earliest recoverable text.
cruxes.if_no: One would have to artificially define 'minor variants' to include 12-verse narrative blocks, rendering the claim circular.
cruxes.your_view: These pericopes are substantial narrative episodes; their presence or absence fundamentally alters the endings and characterizations within the Gospels.

cruxes.crux: Can modern critical Bibles be said to reproduce the 'earliest recoverable form' of the Old Testament when they primarily translate the medieval Masoretic Text?
cruxes.if_yes: One must maintain that the proto-Masoretic tradition alone represents the true original, dismissing the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint as defective corruptions.
cruxes.if_no: One acknowledges that Hebrew manuscript evidence demonstrates ancient pluriformity and that modern Bibles print a late rabbinic standardization rather than an eclectic critical text of earlier editions.
cruxes.your_view: Qumran research (Tov, Ulrich) has settled this empirically: Hebrew Scripture existed in multiple authorized literary editions, and modern translations print the Masoretic tradition for liturgical and practical reasons, not because it is always the earliest recoverable form.

strongest_for: The New Testament possesses an unparalleled wealth of manuscript evidence (over 5,800 Greek manuscripts, thousands of ancient translations) allowing cross-textual genealogical reconstruction with precision unmatched by any other ancient literature.

The Dead Sea Scrolls prove that the proto-Masoretic consonantal text was transmitted with astonishing precision for over a millennium between the 2nd century BCE and the 10th-century Leningrad Codex (e.g., the Great Isaiah Scroll, 1QIsa^a).
Over 90% of all recorded textual variants are completely inconsequential orthographic differences, spelling slips, or untranslatable word-order shifts.
No primary theological dogma of orthodox Christianity (such as the deity of Christ, the resurrection, or justification by faith) depends exclusively on a disputed textual variant.
strongest_against: Famous, substantive stories—most notably the Woman Caught in Adultery (John 7:53-8:11) and the post-resurrection signs and appearances in Mark 16:9-20—are demonstrably late scribal interpolations.

Modern translations of the Hebrew Bible rely overwhelmingly on a diplomatic edition of a single medieval manuscript (the Leningrad Codex, 1008 CE) rather than an eclectic critical reconstruction of the earliest recoverable text.

The Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint reveal that several Old Testament books (e.g., Jeremiah, Samuel, Exodus) existed in distinct developmental editions; modern Bibles translate the longer, secondary edition of Jeremiah rather than the earlier, shorter edition.

Specific doctrinal and ethical passages are altered by variants, including explicit statements on the Trinity (1 John 5:7-8), Christological titles (John 1:18, 1 Tim 3:16), and Jesus' emotional disposition (Mark 1:41).

A chronological gap of decades (NT) to centuries (OT) separates the authorial compositions from our earliest surviving physical manuscripts, during which earliest copying and redaction took place without surviving manuscript witnesses.

for: Citing the sheer number of New Testament manuscripts (5,800+ Greek copies) as proof of original accuracy, ignoring that 80-90% are late medieval Byzantine minuscules that merely duplicate an already standardized ecclesiastical text.

Claiming that the Dead Sea Scrolls prove 'word-for-word identical transmission' across the entire Old Testament, which ignores that Qumran also revealed dramatic textual pluriformity and divergent literary editions.
Asserting that textual variants 'do not affect any doctrine at all', which conflates systemic dogmas across the whole canon with the doctrinal content of individual verses.
against: The 'telephone game' analogy, which falsely compares careful, multi-branched written textual transmission with parallel manuscript lines to a single, linear chain of oral whispers.
Sensationalist claims that the Council of Nicaea or Emperor Constantine radically forged or rewritten the New Testament, refuted by papyri (P45, P46, P66, P75) that predate Nicaea by over a century.
Citing the count of 'over 400,000 textual variants' as evidence of total chaos, when the vast majority are spelling slips, movable nus, and trivial scribal idiosyncrasies.

would_change: Discovery of 1st-century New Testament manuscripts containing the Pericope Adulterae (John 7:53-8:11) or the Longer Ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) in their canonical contexts.

The publication and widespread adoption by modern Bible translation committees of a truly eclectic critical Hebrew Bible (such as the Oxford Hebrew Bible project) that routinely replaces secondary Masoretic readings with earlier Qumran/Septuagint editions.
Discovery of pre-2nd-century papyri demonstrating that New Testament texts underwent radical, systematic theological rewriting during the apostolic and sub-apostolic eras.
Evidence showing that the proto-Masoretic text was an unbroken, uniquely original stream and that divergent Qumran and Septuagint readings were merely sectarian corruptions.

sources.citation: Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament: Its Transmission, Corruption, and Restoration (4th ed., Oxford University Press, 2005)
Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (3rd ed., Fortress Press, 2012)
Eugene Ulrich, The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Developmental Composition of the Bible (Brill, 2015)
Bart D. Ehrman, The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture: The Effect of Early Christological Controversies on the Text of the New Testament (Oxford University Press, 1993/2011)
Daniel B. Wallace (ed.), Revisiting the Corruption of the New Testament: Manuscript, Patristic, and Apocryphal Evidence (Kregel Academic, 2011)
Ronald Hendel, The Oxford Hebrew Bible: Prologue to a New Critical Edition, Vetus Testamentum 58.3 (2008)

analyses.label: Gemini 3.8

analyses.verdict: Probably not true as stated: strong for most New Testament books, not for every book of the Bible.
analyses.bottom_line: The sentence is scored in its natural strict sense: for each biblical book, standard modern critical texts match the earliest recoverable form, and the only leftovers are minor variants that change neither teaching nor story. That is largely right for the New Testament, where Nestle-Aland/UBS is a real reconstruction and most variation is trivial. It is not right for the Hebrew Bible, whose standard critical editions print the medieval Masoretic Text rather than a reconstructed earliest edition, and where some books survive in substantially different ancient forms. A few New Testament variants also change a local story detail or teaching nuance even though they do not rewrite Christianity. A softer claim—that critical Bibles preserve the substance of the books unusually well, and that no core doctrine rests on a doubtful reading—would score much higher, roughly 70.

sub_claims.claim: For each New Testament book, Nestle-Aland 28 / UBS5 closely reproduces the earliest form recoverable from the surviving tradition.
sub_claims.case_for: The New Testament is the best-attested writing complex from Greco-Roman antiquity. Substantial papyri begin in the second and third centuries, Vaticanus and Sinaiticus provide fourth-century full Bibles, and versions plus patristic citations add independent checks. The critical text is eclectic, not a reprint of one late manuscript, and the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method now aims explicitly at the Ausgangstext, the earliest text recoverable from the tradition. Where the famous long additions are secondary, critical editions already omit or bracket them.
sub_claims.case_against: The Ausgangstext is an editorial hypothesis, not a recovered autograph, and it can still move: NA28 changed the wording of the Catholic Epistles in dozens of places relative to NA27. Acts and the Gospels have a persistent Western tradition with real narrative pluses. In a minority of variation units the earliest reading remains genuinely uncertain, so the printed line is the best hypothesis rather than a demonstrated transcription of one ancestor.
sub_claims.consensus: Broad agreement among New Testament textual critics, including confessional scholars such as Daniel Wallace and mainline or secular scholars such as Metzger, Holmes, Parker, and Ehrman, that the earliest attainable text can be reconstructed with high confidence for the great majority of the wording. They divide on how much the residual uncertainty matters, not on whether the critical text is basically the right target.
evidence: P66 and P75, second- or third-century witnesses to John and Luke/John, already stand close to the later Alexandrian text of Vaticanus
Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11 are absent from the earliest Greek witnesses and are bracketed or omitted in critical texts
The Comma Johanneum in 1 John 5:7-8 is absent from the early Greek tradition and is not printed as original
NA28 adopts the Editio Critica Maior text of the Catholic Epistles, showing both stability and ongoing small revision
About 5,500 Greek manuscripts, plus Latin, Syriac, Coptic, and other versions, make large undetected rewriting after the second century unlikely
sub_claims.verdict: Largely true

sub_claims.claim: Remaining New Testament variants are only minor and change no teaching and no story.
sub_claims.case_for: Most variants are spelling, word order, articles, or synonymous phrasing. The longest secondary passages are already marked, so they are not silent parts of the critical text. No central Christian claim—crucifixion, resurrection, worship of Jesus, or the basic ethic of the letters—depends on a reading that exists in only one late branch. Confessional critics are right that popular lists of variants rarely touch a doctrine that is taught in only one doubtful verse.
sub_claims.case_against: The claim says teaching or story, not merely cardinal doctrine. Real variants change local meaning: Mark 1:41 has ancient support for both 'moved with compassion' and 'became angry'; John 1:18 divides between 'Son' and 'God'; Luke 22:43-44 adds or omits the angel and the bloody sweat; Romans 5:1 divides between 'we have peace' and 'let us have peace'; 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 may be an interpolation affecting a teaching about women. Ehrman and Parker have shown that some changes were theologically motivated. Those are not all trivial, even if they are few.
sub_claims.consensus: Scholars agree most variants are insignificant and that the books' overall plots are stable. Evangelical textual critics stress that no essential doctrine is overturned. Ehrman, Parker, and Epp stress that some variants are meaningful, interpretive, and occasionally doctrinal. There is no consensus that literally no teaching or story detail is affected.
evidence: Mark 1:41 compassion/anger is a sense-changing early variant, discussed by Metzger and Ehrman
Luke 22:43-44 and Luke 23:34 are famous uncertain narrative-theological passages
John 1:18 monogenes theos versus monogenes huios changes a christological wording
1 Corinthians 14:34-35 is treated by some critics as a later insertion but is still in the main text of standard editions
Metzger's Textual Commentary documents many variants that affect translation, not just orthography
sub_claims.verdict: Overstated

sub_claims.claim: The main text of standard critical Hebrew Bibles reproduces the earliest recoverable form of each Old Testament book.
sub_claims.case_for: The Masoretic Text is not a medieval invention. Qumran already preserves a proto-Masoretic tradition in the late Second Temple period, and for books such as Isaiah and much of the Torah the medieval text is remarkably close to manuscripts a thousand years older. Careful Masoretic copying, the apparatus of BHS/BHQ, and occasional emendations in translations such as the NRSV mean a reader can often get back to a very early form. For many books the printed Masoretic text may in fact be the earliest recoverable edition.
sub_claims.case_against: BHS and BHQ are diplomatic editions of the Leningrad Codex (1008 CE), not eclectic reconstructions of an Ausgangstext. They print one ancient textual tradition as the text and relegate others to the apparatus. That is a different project from Nestle-Aland. Where Qumran and the Septuagint preserve another literary edition, the main text of a standard critical Bible is not 'the' earliest recoverable form. The unfinished Hebrew Bible: A Critical Edition project exists precisely because the field does not think BHS already is that reconstruction.
sub_claims.consensus: Hebrew Bible textual critics, including Emanuel Tov and Eugene Ulrich, agree that the Masoretic Text is a major ancient witness and often a good one, and they do not agree that it is the earliest form of every book. Confessional Jewish and many evangelical Christian readers privilege the Masoretic Text as the received text; that is a canonical judgment, not the same as a historical claim about the earliest recoverable edition.
evidence: BHS uses Codex Leningradensis, dated 1008, as its printed base
Qumran biblical manuscripts fall into more than one textual group: proto-Masoretic, pre-Samaritan, texts close to the Septuagint Vorlage, and non-aligned texts, in Tov's classification
4QJer^b and 4QJer^d agree with the shorter Septuagint form of Jeremiah against the Masoretic arrangement and length
4QSam^a often agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic text in Samuel
The Hebrew Bible: A Critical Edition, edited under Ronald Hendel, was launched to produce an eclectic text rather than another diplomatic Masoretic edition
sub_claims.verdict: Not true as a claim about each book

sub_claims.claim: Differences among the Masoretic Text, Dead Sea Scrolls, and Septuagint are minor and do not change teaching or story.
sub_claims.case_for: A large share of Dead Sea Scrolls variants are orthographic or grammatical. The Great Isaiah Scroll tells the same book as Masoretic Isaiah. The laws, narratives, and prophetic message of most books remain recognizable across the witnesses. 'Minor' is fair for the modal variant, and proto-Masoretic copies show that the familiar text was already stable before the turn of the era for much of the corpus.
sub_claims.case_against: Edition-level differences are not minor. Septuagint Jeremiah is on the order of one-eighth shorter and differently ordered, and Qumran fragments confirm that this was a Hebrew edition, not a translator's whim. Greek Esther and Greek Daniel contain large narrative additions absent from the Masoretic books. Septuagint Job is substantially shorter. Samuel has numerous readings that change narrative detail, some of which look earlier than the Masoretic wording. Calling all of this 'variants that change no teaching or story' is false.
sub_claims.consensus: Specialists agree the differences range from trivial spelling to alternate literary editions. There is no serious consensus that all cross-witness differences are minor. Confessional defenses of the Masoretic Text usually argue that it is the canonical or the best text, not that the other ancient editions do not exist.
evidence: 1QIsa^a is close to Masoretic Isaiah in content but not identical
Septuagint Jeremiah is substantially shorter and rearranged; 4QJer^b/d support a Hebrew short edition
Septuagint Esther and Daniel include narrative additions that became deuterocanonical in some churches and are absent from the Hebrew Bible
The Old Greek and Masoretic texts of Samuel-Kings diverge in many narrative details
The Samaritan Pentateuch preserves an expansionist Torah edition, sometimes aligned with Qumran Exodus manuscripts
sub_claims.verdict: False for a significant minority of books

sub_claims.claim: Critical Bibles have successfully flagged the major later additions instead of silently treating them as original.
sub_claims.case_for: This is the strongest practical support for the claim. The long ending of Mark, the Pericope Adulterae, and the Comma Johanneum are the passages most often used to argue that the Bible was rewritten, and modern critical texts identify all three as secondary or at least textually doubtful. That is accuracy to the earliest recoverable form, not corruption of it. Modern translations typically footnote them. The same documentary habit—print the earliest attainable text, show the alternatives—is what textual criticism can actually deliver.
sub_claims.case_against: Flagging the famous additions does not settle smaller sense-changing variants, which often remain in the main text with only an apparatus note that ordinary readers never see. In the Old Testament, alternate editions are usually not presented as alternate books; the Masoretic form is simply printed. 'Critical Bible' in a church pew can still mean a translation that follows the Masoretic Text almost everywhere and the Textus Receptus nowhere, without showing the reader that Jeremiah had another ancient shape.
sub_claims.consensus: Agreement is strong that the three famous New Testament additions are secondary or highly doubtful. Agreement is weaker that ordinary critical translations transparently present Old Testament edition-level evidence.
evidence: UBS and Nestle-Aland mark Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11 with double brackets or equivalent doubt signals
The Comma Johanneum is absent from the main text of modern critical Greek editions
NRSV and similar translations footnote these passages while still printing a Masoretic Jeremiah
Reader-facing Bibles rarely print the short Jeremiah as the text of the book
sub_claims.verdict: Largely true for famous New Testament additions; weak for Old Testament editions

sub_claims.claim: Each biblical book has one earliest recoverable form, and modern critical Bibles are printing that form.
sub_claims.case_for: For many books the tradition converges. A working singular initial text is a coherent editorial goal, and for the New Testament the field has operationalized it. Even in the Hebrew Bible, 'earliest recoverable' can mean the earliest form we can reconstruct for the Masoretic edition, which critical tools do approximate. The claim does not require the lost authorial draft, only the earliest form the evidence can reach.
sub_claims.case_against: Fluid composition and multiple authorized editions break the singular. Parker called the Gospels a living text; Ulrich and Tov describe parallel literary editions rather than one line of scribal typos. If two second-century-BCE forms of Jeremiah are both recoverable, printing one of them is not yet recovering 'the' earliest form. Canon adds a further definition problem: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Greek editions and deuterocanonical books whose earliest recoverable forms are a different textual problem from the Hebrew Masoretic books.
sub_claims.consensus: New Testament editors mostly still seek one initial text, with public caveats. Hebrew Bible specialists are divided, with a strong pluralist wing. Confessional communities often define the target as the received canonical text, which answers a different question from the historical one the claim asks.
evidence: NA28's editors describe their goal as the initial text of the tradition, not a guaranteed autograph in every variation unit
Ulrich's work on Qumran argues for successive literary editions of biblical books
Esther and Daniel circulate in more than one ancient book-form
Different churches' canons already select different editions of some books
sub_claims.verdict: Only partly true; the singular target fails for several books

cruxes.crux: Does 'change no teaching or story' mean no local nuance at all, or only no core doctrine and no overall plot?
cruxes.if_yes: If it means no local teaching or story detail whatever, the claim is false; several well-known variants change a scene, a christological wording, or a command.
cruxes.if_no: If it means no core doctrine and no overall narrative, the New Testament half becomes much easier to accept and overall credence rises toward roughly 70.
cruxes.your_view: The sentence says teaching or story, not cardinal doctrine. Local changes count against it. I will not quietly rewrite the claim into the softer slogan.

cruxes.crux: Do 'modern critical Bibles' print a reconstructed earliest text, or the Masoretic Text with a critical apparatus?
cruxes.if_yes: If the phrase means a completed eclectic Hebrew edition plus Nestle-Aland, the Old Testament half is an unfinished project and the claim is premature rather than simply false.
cruxes.if_no: If it means BHS/BHQ and ordinary critical translations, those Old Testament texts are diplomatic or Masoretic-based, so they do not by design reproduce the earliest recoverable form of every book.
cruxes.your_view: In ordinary use the phrase means Nestle-Aland/UBS and BHS/BHQ-based Bibles, not the incomplete Hebrew Bible: A Critical Edition. That reading makes the Old Testament half fail.

cruxes.crux: Are some non-Masoretic ancient editions earlier, or at least not the form printed as the text, in ways that change the book?
cruxes.if_yes: Then 'each book' is false. Jeremiah's short edition and a set of Samuel readings are enough; Esther and Daniel make the problem sharper.
cruxes.if_no: If the Masoretic form is always the earliest recoverable edition and other forms are later or translational, the Old Testament half largely stands.
cruxes.your_view: The evidence is lopsided against 'always.' The short Hebrew Jeremiah is real, and it is not what standard critical Bibles print as the book.

cruxes.crux: Should the received canonical text be the target, rather than the historically earliest recoverable form?
cruxes.if_yes: A confessional prior can save a cousin of the claim by treating the Masoretic Text or the ecclesiastical New Testament as the text that matters, but that is a different claim from the one stated.
cruxes.if_no: If the target is historical, Qumran, the Septuagint, and the early papyri outrank later received forms wherever they preserve an earlier reading or edition.
cruxes.your_view: The claim itself names the earliest recoverable form, so the historical target is the one being scored. Canonical reception is a value judgment and does not make the historical sentence true.

strongest_for: The New Testament critical text is a disciplined reconstruction from early and abundant witnesses, not a medieval reprint, and it is stable across the vast majority of the wording.
The variants most often cited as proof of rewriting—the long ending of Mark, the Pericope Adulterae, and the Comma Johanneum—are exactly the ones critical Bibles already mark as secondary.
Dead Sea Scrolls showed that the Masoretic tradition is ancient; for books such as Isaiah the familiar text was already substantially in place before the Common Era.

Relative to other ancient literature, both Testaments are unusually well documented, and large post-second-century invention of whole books would be visible in the papyri, versions, or Qumran evidence.
The claim wisely says 'earliest recoverable form' rather than 'autograph,' which is the only target textual criticism can actually hit.
strongest_against: Standard critical Hebrew Bibles print Leningrad Codex, a medieval Masoretic manuscript, rather than an eclectic earliest text of each book.
Jeremiah, Samuel, Esther, Daniel, and Job show differences of length, order, or narrative content that are not minor variants.
Some New Testament variants change a local teaching or story detail, so the clause 'change no teaching or story' is stronger than the evidence.
'Each book' is a universal. A handful of clear exceptions falsifies it even if most books pass.
Where two ancient editions are both recoverable, there is often no demonstrated singular earliest form for a critical Bible to reproduce.

for: 'There are thousands of manuscripts, so the text must be pure.' Quantity documents the tradition; it does not by itself prove that the printed text is the earliest form, and most New Testament manuscripts are late Byzantine copies.

The slogan that the text is 99 percent pure, or that agreement among manuscripts proves verbatim originals. Percentage-of-letters figures inflate stability, are often poorly defined, and do not address edition-level Old Testament differences.
'No doctrine is affected, therefore no teaching or story is affected.' Those are different claims. The first is defensible; the second is what the sentence actually says.
Treating a critical translation's English main text as if it were a settled original-language reconstruction of every Old Testament book.
against: The telephone-game analogy. Biblical books were copied by scribes from exemplars, often with correction, not whispered serially; comparison across independent copies detects most later changes.
'Hundreds of thousands of variants mean the text is unknowable.' Variant counts rise with the number of manuscripts, and most entries are spelling, nonsense, or singular slips.
'Constantine or Nicaea rewrote the Bible.' The council did not produce the critical text, and second- and third-century papyri already contain the substance of the New Testament books.

'We lack the autographs, so we have no idea what the books said.' The claim is about the earliest recoverable form. Absence of the author's copy does not erase early manuscripts or make reconstruction impossible.

would_change: A completed, widely adopted eclectic Hebrew Bible showing that, book by book, the earliest recoverable edition matches the Masoretic text except in minor variants.
Early manuscripts showing large, previously undetected rewriting of many New Testament books after the initial text, beyond the known doubtful passages.
A strong demonstration that the short Jeremiah and the major non-Masoretic Samuel readings are secondary rather than earlier or parallel ancient editions.

Restating the claim as 'no core doctrine or overall narrative depends on a textually doubtful passage, and critical editions are highly reliable guides to an early text'—that different sentence would move my credence to roughly 70.
Discovery of very early extensive manuscripts that systematically confirm or overturn the sense-changing readings now left uncertain in the apparatus.

sources.citation: Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament: Its Transmission, Corruption, and Restoration, 4th ed. (2005)

analyses.label: Grok 4.7

analyses.verdict: Largely true for the New Testament, false as a blanket claim for 'each book' because of the Hebrew Bible
analyses.bottom_line: The New Testament is the best-attested text from antiquity. Modern critical editions (NA28/UBS5) almost certainly match the earliest recoverable text except in a small number of places, and the famous late additions (the long ending of Mark, the woman caught in adultery, the Johannine Comma) are already bracketed or removed. A few unresolved NT variants do touch story or emphasis, but no major doctrine rests on them alone. The Hebrew Bible is different. Standard critical Hebrew Bibles (BHS, BHQ) are diplomatic editions that print a single medieval Masoretic manuscript. The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint show that for several books (Jeremiah, Samuel, Ezekiel, parts of Exodus, Esther, Daniel) an earlier or different literary edition is recoverable and differs in content and narrative, not just spelling. Read strictly, as covering every book, the claim fails. Read as covering only the NT, or as aiming at the canonical Masoretic form rather than the earliest form, it scores much better: roughly 60-70 for the NT alone.

sub_claims.claim: The modern critical Greek New Testament (NA28/UBS5, ECM) closely reproduces the earliest recoverable (Initial) text, with remaining uncertainties affecting no teaching or story.
sub_claims.case_for: There are over 5,000 Greek manuscripts, early papyri (P45, P46, P66, P75) from the 2nd-3rd centuries, early versions, and patristic citations. The great majority of the roughly 500,000 non-spelling variants are trivial. CBGM-based ECM editions report few changes from NA27 and quantify coherence. The best-known substantive interpolations are already marked as secondary. Even skeptical scholars such as Ehrman concede that no essential doctrine depends on a disputed variant.
sub_claims.case_against: A handful of viable variants do affect narrative or theology. Examples: Luke 22:43-44 (Jesus sweating blood), Luke 23:34a (the forgiveness prayer), Mark 1:41 (anger vs compassion), Hebrews 2:9 ('apart from God' vs 'by the grace of God'), John 1:18 ('only God' vs 'only Son'), Matthew 24:36 ('nor the Son'), Mark 1:1 ('Son of God'), and possibly 1 Cor 14:34-35. The Western text of Acts is about 8 percent longer. The gap between the autographs and the earliest copies (often a century or more) is real, though it sits outside this claim.
sub_claims.consensus: Broad agreement across evangelical (Wallace, Gurry, Hixson), mainstream (Metzger, Holmes), and skeptical (Ehrman) scholars that the critical text is very close to the Initial Text. The scholars disagree on how much the residual variants matter. Some (Parker, Epp) question whether 'original text' is even the right goal.
evidence: P66 and P75 (c. 200) closely agree with Codex Vaticanus in John and Luke
NA28 brackets Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11
ECM Acts and Catholic Letters introduced only a few dozen changes
Luke 22:43-44 is absent from P75, Vaticanus, and others
sub_claims.verdict: Mostly true; a small number of open variants carry modest narrative or theological weight

sub_claims.claim: The proto-Masoretic consonantal text has been transmitted with very high fidelity from the late Second Temple period to modern printed Hebrew Bibles.
sub_claims.case_for: Proto-MT scrolls from Qumran, Masada, and Wadi Murabba'at (e.g., 1QIsa-b, the Masada scrolls) agree closely with medieval codices such as Aleppo and Leningrad across more than 1,000 years. Even the fuller 1QIsa-a differs mostly in spelling and minor readings.
sub_claims.case_against: Fidelity within one tradition does not show that the tradition is the earliest text. The MT also contains recognized corruptions that were faithfully copied, such as the defective Saul regnal formula in 1 Sam 13:1.
sub_claims.consensus: Strong consensus, including Tov, Ulrich, and confessional scholars, that MT transmission was highly conservative from about the 1st century CE.
evidence: 1QIsa-a vs Leningrad Codex
Masada and Murabba'at scrolls aligned with MT
Leningrad Codex dated 1008 CE
sub_claims.verdict: True

sub_claims.claim: Modern critical Hebrew Bibles reproduce the earliest recoverable form of each Hebrew Bible book.
sub_claims.case_for: For many books (e.g., Genesis apart from the chronologies, Isaiah, Psalms, most of the Torah) the MT is probably close to the earliest recoverable text. Modern translations such as the NRSV(ue) adopt some Qumran and LXX readings. The eclectic HBCE project explicitly aims at an earliest-text reconstruction.
sub_claims.case_against: BHS and BHQ print the Leningrad Codex and put alternatives in the apparatus. Several books survive in variant literary editions. LXX Jeremiah is about one-seventh shorter with a different order, supported by 4QJer-b,d. LXX 1 Samuel 17-18 lacks much of the David-Goliath doublet. In Papyrus 967, Ezekiel lacks 36:23c-38 and orders chapters differently. Exodus 35-40, Joshua, 1 Kings, Esther, and Daniel also differ. The Genesis 5 and 11 chronologies differ by centuries across MT, SP, and LXX. Samuel's MT is widely judged corrupt in places, for example the Nahash passage preserved in 4QSam-a. Deut 32:8 reads 'sons of Israel' in MT where 4QDeut-j and the LXX have 'sons of God'.
sub_claims.consensus: Leading textual critics (Tov, Ulrich, Hendel, Lange) agree that the MT is not uniformly the earliest text and that several books show multiple editions. Some confessional scholars favor MT priority more often, but few deny the Jeremiah and Samuel data.
evidence: 4QJer-b and LXX Jeremiah
4QSam-a
4QDeut-j at Deut 32:8
Papyrus 967 (Ezekiel)
LXX 1 Sam 17-18 short form
sub_claims.verdict: False as a general claim

sub_claims.claim: Where critical texts may diverge from the earliest form, the differences never affect teaching or story.
sub_claims.case_for: No creedal doctrine rests solely on a disputed reading. Most HB edition differences concern arrangement, expansion, or harmonization rather than theology.
sub_claims.case_against: Several differences change narrative content or theological picture. Examples: the shape of the David-Goliath story, the content and order of Jeremiah, Deut 32:8's divine council, Ezekiel 36-39's order, the Greek additions to Esther, and in the NT Luke 22:43-44 and Mark 1:41. The 'no teaching or story' clause is the strongest part of the claim and the most vulnerable.
sub_claims.consensus: No consensus; this depends on how 'teaching' and 'story' are defined. Apologetic writers stress doctrinal stability. Textual critics generally say some variants are meaningful.
evidence: Deut 32:8
Jeremiah editions
Mark 1:41
sub_claims.verdict: False on a natural reading; true only if 'teaching' means core creedal doctrine

sub_claims.claim: 'Earliest recoverable form' is a single, well-defined target for every biblical book.
sub_claims.case_for: For most NT books the CBGM 'Initial Text' is a workable, operational target, and for many HB books a single archetype is plausible.
sub_claims.case_against: Where books grew through successive editions (Jeremiah, Samuel, Ezekiel, Esther, Daniel, possibly Acts), the 'earliest recoverable' edition and the 'canonical' edition diverge. Ulrich's pluriformity model treats several forms as authoritative simultaneously.
sub_claims.consensus: Contested: Tov has shifted toward accepting multiple editions; Ulrich emphasizes pluriformity; Epp and Parker critique a single 'original text' for the NT.
evidence: Epp 1999 on 'original text'
Ulrich's developmental composition model
CBGM Ausgangstext concept
sub_claims.verdict: Workable for most books, problematic for several

cruxes.crux: Does the claim cover the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament (and deuterocanon), not just the New Testament?
cruxes.if_yes: The claim fails because of the Jeremiah, Samuel, Ezekiel, and Esther editions and the diplomatic nature of BHS/BHQ; credence around 10-20.
cruxes.if_no: For the NT alone, the claim is largely true; credence around 60-70.
cruxes.your_view: 'Each book' and 'Bible' imply the whole canon, so I score the inclusive reading.

cruxes.crux: Is the target the earliest recoverable literary edition, or the final canonical edition?
cruxes.if_yes: If earliest edition, the MT-based critical texts miss it for several HB books.
cruxes.if_no: If canonical (MT) edition, the HB scores much better, though residual MT corruptions in Samuel and elsewhere remain.
cruxes.your_view: The claim explicitly says 'earliest recoverable form', which points to the stricter reading.

cruxes.crux: Do variants such as Deut 32:8, 1 Sam 17-18, Luke 22:43-44, and Mark 1:41 count as changing 'teaching or story'?
cruxes.if_yes: The no-impact clause fails even for the NT, though narrowly.
cruxes.if_no: Only creedal-level differences count; the NT easily passes, and the HB edition differences still strain the clause.
cruxes.your_view: Under ordinary usage, at least some of these change story details or theological emphasis.

cruxes.crux: Does marking a reading as doubtful in brackets or apparatus count as accurately reproducing the earliest form?
cruxes.if_yes: The NT critical text scores higher, since most major problems are flagged.
cruxes.if_no: Every bracketed or uncertain reading counts as a potential miss.
cruxes.your_view: Flagging is reasonable credit for the NT, but BHS's main text plainly prints the MT edition of Jeremiah and Samuel.

cruxes.crux: Was the NT text stable in the largely undocumented 1st-2nd centuries?
cruxes.if_yes: The 'earliest recoverable' text is likely close to the autographs, though that lies outside this claim.
cruxes.if_no: Fidelity to the earliest recoverable text still holds, but that text could differ from what the authors wrote.
cruxes.your_view: Evidence for 2nd-century stability is moderate, not conclusive; this affects the 'original text' question more than this claim.

strongest_for: The NT has unparalleled manuscript attestation, including very early papyri that closely match critical-text readings.
The best-known substantive NT interpolations are already excluded or bracketed in critical editions.
The proto-MT tradition shows remarkable copying fidelity over a millennium, as confirmed by Qumran and Masada.
Even skeptical scholars concede that no central doctrine depends on a disputed variant.
CBGM provides a rigorous, transparent method for reconstructing the NT Initial Text.
strongest_against: Critical Hebrew Bibles (BHS, BHQ) print one medieval manuscript; they do not reconstruct the earliest text.
Jeremiah, Samuel, Ezekiel, Exodus 35-40, Esther, and Daniel survive in distinct literary editions with substantive narrative differences.
Specific readings with theological weight, such as Deut 32:8, likely have an earlier form than the MT preserves.
Several unresolved NT variants (Luke 22:43-44, Mark 1:41, Heb 2:9, John 1:18) carry narrative or theological significance.
The deuterocanonical books (e.g., Tobit's two Greek recensions) add further textual pluriformity.

for: 'The NT is 99.5% pure' figures: they are popular approximations rather than rigorous measures, and they say nothing about the Hebrew Bible.
'The Dead Sea Scrolls proved the OT unchanged': they confirmed the proto-MT's stability but also revealed different editions and non-MT readings.
'More manuscripts than any other ancient text, therefore accurate': quantity alone does not settle early variation or which edition is earliest.
against: 'There are more variants than words in the NT': most variants are spelling or trivial, and the count rises because there are so many manuscripts.
'The Bible is a translation of a translation': modern translations work directly from Hebrew and Greek critical texts.
'Constantine or the Council of Nicaea rewrote the Bible': no manuscript evidence supports this, and pre-Nicene papyri match later texts.

would_change: Clear evidence that MT readings are primary in Jeremiah and Samuel, contrary to 4QJer-b and 4QSam-a.
A completed, widely accepted eclectic Hebrew critical edition (e.g., HBCE) adopted as the standard critical Bible.
New early papyri resolving key NT variants such as Luke 22:43-44 or Mark 1:41.
A consensus that 'earliest recoverable form' should mean the canonical edition for multi-edition books.
Discovery of 1st-century NT manuscripts showing significant divergence from the critical text.

analyses.label: Opus 5.5

synthesis.summary: All four reviewers judge the claim too strong, while agreeing that much biblical text is well preserved and most variants are small. They agree that some variants affect narrative details or the wording of passages with theological significance, even if no central doctrine depends solely on a disputed reading. They distinguish the generally well-supported New Testament critical text from standard Hebrew critical editions that print a Masoretic manuscript while recording alternatives. All note that some biblical books circulated in substantially different ancient forms, complicating the search for a single earliest form. They differ in confidence, in how strongly they describe particular reconstructions, and in how much credit to give editions that mark disputed material.
agreed: The claim fails as a blanket statement about every book and every meaningful variant.
Most identifiable variants are minor, and manuscript comparison supports substantial confidence in much of the text.
Some variants affect stories or theological wording; this is distinct from overturning a core doctrine.
Major New Testament additions such as Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11 are bracketed or otherwise flagged in critical editions.
Standard Hebrew critical editions print a Masoretic manuscript, while ancient witnesses preserve other substantive readings and literary forms.
The earliest recoverable text is not necessarily identical to the lost authorial original.

disagreed.positions: GPT-6.1 assigns the overall claim 8, Opus 5.5 assigns 17, and Gemini 3.8 and Grok 4.7 each assign 25. Gemini reports high confidence; the other three report medium confidence.

disagreed.point: How to assess disputed New Testament passages in modern editions
disagreed.positions: GPT-6.1 scores the printed main text and treats even qualified inclusion as potentially relevant, while emphasizing that brackets matter. Grok and Opus give substantial credit for bracketed or removed additions; Gemini emphasizes their substantive impact as textual additions.

disagreed.point: How firmly earlier forms can be identified
disagreed.positions: Gemini treats the shorter Jeremiah edition as earlier and the longer Masoretic edition as secondary. Grok and Opus emphasize earlier or distinct editions, while GPT-6.1 stresses that some rankings remain genuinely contested and that a variant alone does not establish which reading is earliest.

Gemini estimates more than 90% of the New Testament text is firmly established. Grok and Opus emphasize high confidence in most wording but caution against poorly defined purity percentages; GPT-6.1 gives no comparable percentage.

deciding_cruxes: Whether 'teaching or story' includes changes to individual statements and episodes or only to core doctrines and overall plots.
Whether the object assessed is the printed main text alone or the edition together with brackets and notes.
Whether the target is the earliest recoverable literary form, a received canonical edition, or the lost authorial original.
Whether the evidence establishes which competing reading or edition is earlier in each disputed case.
Whether the claim covers the whole Bible or only the New Testament.
synthesis.what_is_settled: Across the reviews, the shared conclusion is that much wording is well preserved, most variants are minor, and some are substantive. Modern critical editions flag prominent New Testament additions, while standard Hebrew editions print a Masoretic manuscript and document alternatives.
synthesis.what_is_open: The earliest attainable reading remains uncertain in some passages, as does the priority of some ancient editions. The overall assessment also depends on how one defines a changed teaching or story, which canon and textual target are intended, and whether annotations count as part of the text being assessed.
